claims.text: Near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles possess severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion creates high kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Higher barriers to atomic diffusion inhibit phase segregation.
Higher barriers to atomic diffusion inhibit nanoparticle coarsening.
Small deviations from equiatomic composition reduce lattice distortion.
Reduced lattice distortion lowers the activation barrier for atom migration.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles are more susceptible to thermally driven instability than equiatomic nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy is associated with a highly distorted lattice in the proposed initial nanoparticles.
Strict equiatomic composition maximizes lattice distortion.
High-resolution TEM or atom-probe tomography can measure lattice distortion and detect elemental segregation or phase separation.
Slower atomic diffusion retards phase separation at high temperature.
Equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve a uniform elemental distribution and single-phase structure during high-temperature service.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will develop phase segregation or secondary phases earlier than equiatomic nanoparticles.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit greater grain growth than equiatomic nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies when alloying elements have comparable chemical affinities and similar oxidation tendencies.
Environmental oxidation can independently cause nanoparticle degradation.
The sluggish-diffusion effect is well established in bulk high-entropy alloys.
Surface-energy differences and oxidation may contribute to high-temperature nanoparticle instability independently of lattice distortion.
